learningPurpose: Prepare students to recognise pressure as force distributed over area and to use consistent SI units in introductory fluid-pressure reasoning.

definitions.meaning: Force distributed over an area in a fluid or on a surface.

governingPrinciples: Pressure calculations require consistent force and area units.
This file covers introductory static-pressure reasoning only.

sourceReferences.section: Introduction to Pressure in Fluid Mechanics

assumptions: The force is applied normally over the stated area.
The example is educational and not a pressure-vessel design case.
limitations: Does not cover dynamic pressure, compressibility, pipe losses, pressure-vessel design, or equipment ratings.
The cited web edition has no fixed page numbering.

workedExample.title: Pressure from a known force and area
workedExample.purpose: Show the required SI-unit relationship without creating a full lesson.
given: Area is stated in square metres.
steps: Check that force and area are in SI units.
Divide force by area to obtain pressure in pascals.
workedExample.answer: The result is expressed in pascals.

normalOperation: Pressure readings are interpreted only within the stated educational assumptions.
commonMisconceptions: Treating pressure and force as the same quantity.
Entering an area in cm^2 or mm^2 as if it were m^2.
Treating an ideal classroom result as an equipment rating.

faultConditions.title: Unexpected pressure reading
symptoms: The reading is outside the expected training range.
likelyCauses: Sensor or gauge issue in a real system
faultConditions.safeResponse: Treat real-system abnormal pressure as a safety concern and follow supervised laboratory or site procedures.

safety.warning: Real pressurised systems can be hazardous and must not be treated as simple classroom examples.
safety.studentBoundary: Students must not use this lesson as permission to inspect, open, adjust, or operate pressurised equipment.

sourceReferences.section: Introduction to Pressure in Fluid Mechanics
